speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEMORIAL TO HONOUR THE FIRST WOMAN ELECTED TO THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I am very pleased to communicate to the house the decision of the internal economy commission regarding a memorial in honour of the late Agnes Mac-phail.
The commissioners of internal economy have had before them for consideration representations from the lady members of the Senate and House of Commons and from senators and members of parliament generally, as well as from various women's organizations, suggesting that the election to the House of Commons of the first lady member be suitably commemorated.
The commissioners have also been informed that a bronze bust by Felix Weihs de Weldon, sculptor, of Miss Agnes Campbell Macphail, the first woman elected to the House of Commons of Canada, has been graciously offered to the House of Commons by Mrs. Meredith Reany, of Palmerston, Ontario, and Mrs. Hugh Bailey of Toronto, sisters of Miss Macphail.
The commissioners have had this matter under consideration and have recommended: (a) that to commemorate this historic event, a bronze bust of the first woman member, Miss Agnes Macphail, be placed on a pedestal in the vicinity of the chamber of the House of Commons; and (b) that for this purpose the bronze bust of Miss Macphail offered by her two sisters, be gratefully accepted.
Several appropriate dates together with arrangements for the unveiling ceremony are still under consideration and will be announced later.

Order. May I perhaps deal with the point the Leader of the Opposition has made. Paragraph 3 of standing order 31 states, relative to the mover:
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it is in order,-
I think it is in order.
-and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.
Since I gave it as my opinion that I did not think it was of urgent public importance in the sense which has always been adopted in practice, I did not, therefore, read it out, and I am not going to ask whether the member has the leave of the house; and, according to our established practice, the matter must rest there.
In this case I am not deciding on a point of order. I am deciding on practice, and by virtue of this standing order it just so happens that it is up to me to decide whether the motion is of urgent public importance. If I do not think it is of urgent public importance and do not read the motion then it is unnecessary to ask whether the hon. member has the leave of the house.
I agree that in years past the strict procedure with respect to standing order 31 was to the effect that the minute a motion was made the Speaker did not have the opportunity of deciding whether he thought it was of urgent public importance. The burden did not he upon him, and all he had to do was to ask if the hon. member who moved the motion had leave; and if twenty hon. members rose, all the Speaker had to do was to resume his seat and allow the debate to carry on.
However, this standing order was amended in 1927-see Journals, 1927, Tuesday, March 22, page 316 and page 334. Also Hansard, 1927, Tuesday, March 22, page 1426, re: amended rule 39, now standing order 31- and ever since these words have been included, to the effect that the Speaker has to decide whether he thinks it is of urgent public importance, the practice has always been, as established by Mr. Speaker Black and his successors-and I observe that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) recalls the establishment of that

Mr. Speaker, may I make one or two comments on this matter of your decision as to whether this is of urgent public importance. I fully realize that your decision, once made, is final and is not subject to appeal. But all I would ask Your Honour to do is to hear a word or two on this point which may perhaps lead you to reconsider that decision.
I am not going to anticipate what would have been said had you ruled otherwise, but I would ask you to consider whether the possibility of this matter being reached at a later stage today is of sufficient reality to justify your decision, appreciating the possibility that it may not be reached for another couple of days if the supply motion should not be reached today.
With regard to the matter which has been raised, a statement of government policy would be a most urgent and important matter. In view of that, I would refer Your Honour to citation 249 in Beauchesne's second edition. I realize it may not be strictly applicable to the full extent in this house in view of some of the rulings which have been made, but nevertheless I would place it before Your Honour for your consideration. It reads:
In doubtful cases, the question of urgency and of importance are left for the house to decide by giving or withholding its support.
The authority for that citation is the manual of procedure in public business of the British House of Commons and for that reason I fully realize that it may not be applicable in this house, but I take the liberty of suggesting to Your Honour that there is some merit in it, and I hope Your Honour will agree, despite the fact that for the moment you have given the decision that it is not urgent. If the Speaker thinks that the subject matter of the motion is of urgent public importance, standing order 31 provides that he will ascertain whether the member has the leave of the house to move the motion. Urgency within this rule-
That is within standing order 31.

In considering the urgency of debating this motion, having regard to the meaning given to "urgency" in citation 174, I have to examine what is already on the order paper for discussion. There is the measure providing allowances for disabled persons. If I recall the debate which took place on second reading of that measure not long ago, it would seem that is a matter of rather urgent public importance. Then on the orders of the day today the acting leader of the house announced that there would be a motion to go into supply. Having regard to all the remarks that were made on both sides of the house with respect to the possibility of moving to go into supply later this day, I think we might perhaps forgo the discussion of this subject for the present. I feel sure that later in the day an opportunity for discussion will be provided on the motion to go into supply.

The
statement made by the minister when introducing this bill was so comprehensive, Mr. Chairman, that there is very little left that can be usefully said. It is not my intention, therefore, to speak at any length on this

subject but I do welcome the initiative taken by the government in sponsoring this measure. It is, I believe, very significant that the disabled persons measure should be introduced at this time, so soon after a federal election campaign, during which the type of assistance referred to in the bill now before the house was not the subject of any election promise.
I am proud to be a supporter of a government that places such a high priority on human welfare. I am proud, too, that the provincial government of Nova Scotia has signified its intention of participating in this new program, and has, indeed, already passed the necessary legislation.
In fact, this was one of the highlights of the legislation recommended in 1954 by our late beloved premier, Angus L. Macdonald, and was one of the last items approved prior to his untimely passing. I know that I speak for the disabled in my constituency, who will benefit under this legislation, when I commend our Prime Minister for his special interest, in having this legislation brought forward, and his able lieutenant, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, for the part he is playing in sponsoring it.
The disabled in our midst have a very special claim on the sympathies of their more fortunate, able-bodied fellow citizens. There are, unhappily, a good many Canadians who, through no fault of their own, are barred through some disability from playing their full part in the life of the nation. But Canadians can be proud of the steps that have been taken in this country to provide for those unfortunate persons suffering from serious disabilities.
For many groups, such as our war veterans, the blind, and others, provision has already been made, through existing federal, provincial and local programs of one kind or another. A good deal of effective work is also being done by service clubs, and by voluntary agencies, such as the Canadian Arthritis and Rheumatism Society, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, and others.
The rehabilitation of the disabled has also become an important feature in our legislative programs and, indeed, it is generally agreed that Canada's rehabilitation program for disabled veterans equals that of any other country.
Much has been done, also, through the federal Department of Labour, to train handicapped persons, and to place them in useful productive positions, using the facilities of the national employment service.
Through the new civilian rehabilitation branch of the labour department, federal grants have been made available, to support
Disabled Persons-Allowances co-ordinated provincial rehabilitation programs, so that these can achieve maximum coverage and effectiveness. The magnitude of rehabilitation efforts in Canada is indicated by the fact that in 1949 more than 325,000 disabled persons received assistance, under a number of different programs, at a cost of some $110 million.
Then again, since the national health program was instituted in 1948, there has been a continuous increase in the health provisions for our disabled citizens. The crippled children's grant has been extensively r^d for rehabilitation purposes. Under the tuWr-culosis control, and the mental health grants, much has been done for persons handicapped by these diseases, while other grants have assisted the victims of arthritis and polio to win their way back to health. Meanwhile governmental assistance has promoted the construction of additional hospital accommodation and, under the professional training grant, health workers have been trained in the technique of rehabilitation of the disabled.
Last year an important step was taken, with the institution of the medical rehabilitation grant, to extend in every province the provisions for disabled persons.
But, despite all that is being done, there still remains a hitherto neglected group of disabled civilians for whom the community as a whole should be prepared to shoulder a share of the responsibility. These are the men and women who will benefit by this new, nation-wide program of disability allowances.
It is well for every member of this house to remember the terms of the resolution, and the provisions of the bill now before us. I note that the age of eligibility has been set at 18 years, and a residence of 10 years is required. I understand it has been estimated that the number of pensioners to be covered under this legislation will run between 25,000 and 35,000, and that the annual cost will represent an expenditure of $12 million to $16 million.
The bill states quite specifically that assistance will be available to those in need, who are "totally and permanently disabled". It would be most unfortunate if members of this house were to convey to their constituents any false impressions as to the extent of the coverage of the present measure.
Some will say that this bill is unduly restrictive; that eligibility should not be limited so rigidly, to those whose disability is total and permanent. I think, however, that if any member of this house were to take the trouble to examine the provisions of similar legislation in the United States and
5630	HOUSE OF
Disabled Persons

Allowances elsewhere, he would find that the measure now being introduced by this government is equally as generous as any similar program now in existence, anywhere.
It should not be forgotten that the ultimate aim of any forward-looking program, on behalf of the handicapped, should not be merely the provision of financial relief but, rather, victory over the handicap. There are many persons now suffering from a temporary or partial disability who could be helped back to a useful, self-supporting existence. It^/ould then, in my view, be a retrograde st^>
if action were now taken to encourage dependency on the part of those persons for whom rehabilitation may be possible.
Only when it proves impossible to help a disabled person to lead a happy and productive life, through his own endeavours, should we consider the provision of a pension. In such cases a pension will provide a guaranteed level of protection, and will represent a very real advance in establishing security for some thousands of our citizens who, up to this time, have had little or no help under our established programs.
No doubt there will be some who will not be satisfied with the present measure-just as there were some who spoke against family allowances, and every other progressive social measure, introduced by Liberal governments over the past 20 years. I, for one, believe in giving credit where credit is due, and I should therefore like to commend the government upon this important, humane and far-reaching social measure.
Summing up, Mr. Chairman, the social legislation introduced for Canadians, by successive Liberal governments, has provided a degree of security for our elder citizens, and has ensured at least a minimum of wellbeing for the very young; we have shown gratitude to our veterans and their dependents, through unsurpassed veterans legislation; the youth of our country have been assisted in their educational program, through special students grants, vocational training, grants to universities, and so on. Labour legislation has been introduced to make easier the lot of the labouring man. Unemployment insurance benefits are available for those temporarily out of work. Our people, generally, have benefited by extensive health and welfare legislation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have the disabled persons bill, and I am sure that all these other groups of Canadians will welcome this measure with that spirit of generosity towards the needy which has always been characteristic of our citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may deal with these questions now before we pass this clause. I thank members of the committee for their useful suggestions.
First of all, in answer to the hon. member for Prince, I think I should say that I already mentioned in the house in my statement in chief that as far as we were aware enabling legislation had been provided in eight of the 10 provinces. Undoubtedly the impression created by that observation was that in the case of the provinces of Quebec and Prince Edward Island no such enabling legislation existed, and that possibly there was not going to be any support given by these provinces to this measure.
The premier of the government of Prince Edward Island called me on the telephone and pointed out that his government intended to take advantage of this legislation just as
[Mr. Zaplitny.l

quickly as possible. I pointed out to him that there was no enabling legislation in the province of Prince Edward Island and it was because of that that I made the statement to which he had directed my attention.
He intimated that his government had considered the matter and they were of the opinion that no enabling legislation was necessary in that province. He assured me without reservation that Prince Edward Island was going to join the scheme. I can therefore now say that there are nine provinces which will undoubtedly take advantage of the legislation, and I am hopeful that all the provinces in Canada will eventually take advantage.
With regard to the observations made by the hon. member for Dauphin, I think he has made several valuable suggestions, and I can only give him my reaction to them.
With regard to the qualifying residence period of 10 years, the hon. member will note that that is the same period required in the case of blind persons, and as this is disability legislation we are anxious to have both acts conform, one with the other, as closely as possible, consistent with the wishes of the majority of the provinces.
The question of residence was discussed with the provinces and every one of them was of the opinion that this qualifying period of 10 years was desirable. In the case of family allowances there is a lesser period of one year but the circumstances, I think, are different. In any event, this was the wish of most of the provinces. It conformed to our own thinking at the time because of our desire to see that this measure should be as consistent as we could make it with the blindness allowances act.
On the question my hon. friend raised regarding paragraphs (e) and (f), the problems he has noted have been very much in our minds and the reason for (f) is that we hope by regulation-and it is only by regulation that we can deal with this kind of situation- to try to meet the kind of cases he had in mind, and which were also referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. The words "except as prescribed by regulation" in paragraph (f) will mitigate somewhat the exclusive result created by the general terms of paragraph (e).
Much has been made today and last week of the fact that the bill does not define "total and permanent disability." Now, as the hon. member for Prince Albert has pointed out, this is a very difficult matter to define. The hon. member for Lanark thought we should define total and permanent disability in the bill. But I am sure on reflection he would agree that is neither desirable nor possible.

In the Ontario measure, which we have followed very closely, there has not even been an attempt to define it under the regulations as we are going to do. The experience in Ontario has been that it was best not to define it at all. They did not even propose to do it by regulation as we are going to endeavour to do. We have examined the legislation in over 30 states in the United States. Our officers have visited and talked to the officials there, and the vast majority of the states do not in their legislation define total and permanent disability. In one or two instances where it has been defined in the law itself they have got into all sorts of trouble because experience has shown that there is need for change. The best judgment we could get from the states we visited, and from Ontario, Alberta, and Newfoundland, where they have had some experience, was that we should not define it in the bill, except to state it in general terms, and that we should try instead to define it by regulation.
We will do exactly what the hon. member for Prince Albert suggested, namely, we will submit to the provinces a definition for regulation purposes which, of course, will receive their consideration and, we hope, approval.
As I said when I spoke in the house, what we have in mind is a definition along the lines of what they have generally used in Ontario by the use of the words "permanent and total disability". We mean a disability is "permanent" in the sense that it cannot be corrected within the foreseeable future, and we mean "total" in the sense that a person cannot perform the ordinary activities of daily living without the assistance of another person.
In the definition we have in mind we do not intend to have the limitation which now exists in Alberta of a twelve-month period. I think we will have no difficulty, in fact, I know we will have no difficulty, with the province of Alberta in that particular.
In order to give the committee an indication of our intentions as regards the kind of regulation which we hope will represent the wishes of both the provinces and ourselves, I might add that we will mean by "permanent" a disability to which the concept of cure cannot be applied and which is not likely to improve, or which is likely to continue throughout the lifetime of the individual.
That does not mean to say that that necessarily will be the case. It does not mean to say that rehabilitation measures will not be pursued as they are going to be pursued, and as other sections of the act indicate. But that would be a guide.

When we decided on this measure we had to make certain estimates, naturally, as to cost. That is something which it is not very easy to do. However, using the figures in Alberta and in Ontario we roughly concluded that we would be covering a group numbering between 25,000 and 35,000.
The kind of case which my friend, the hon. member for Yorkton, had in mind obviously cannot be covered by this measure. This is a measure for disabled people. However, in the case he mentioned, I am sure that by rehabilitation measures some mitigation of the difficulty could be anticipated.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I need to comment on any further matter that has been raised, except to indicate that there might be in this bill features that would not be there if it were dependent entirely on the act of the federal government alone. We do not want to put in the bill provisions which we know the provinces would be unwilling to accept or which they would find it difficult to accept. With those comments I think I may say that we look forward to this act providing, in co-operation with the provinces, valuable assistance and help to an extremely important group of our people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: On the surface it does seem to be restrictive. The purpose of having in the bill the phrase "as prescribed in the regulations" is to permit giving disability allowances, under certain circumstances, to certain people who are actually assuming the financial responsibility for the care they are receiving. This bill follows the lines of the Ontario act. It is not intended to provide disability allowances to the institutions that are provided for by the community, the municipality or the province. While the provision in paragraph (e) is not as exclusive as that in paragraph (d), nevertheless some of these institutions-hospital, nursing home or private, charitable or public institution-may be institutions providing care to people who are receiving moneys at the public expense. It is not intended to provide disability pensions for them unless they are actually providing for themselves. The only way we can deal with the matter in respect to all the many kinds and varieties of institutions is to wait until we are faced with a particular kind of situation. Without accepting that as a reason for the ten-year requirement being justifiable in either case, may I ask the minister why that argument is not carried over to the question of the division of the costs between the federal government and the provinces? As he knows, under the Blind Persons Act the division is on a 75-25 basis whereas in this legislation, which he characterizes as being comparable to the Blind Persons Act, the split is 50-50. My reasons for urging that the split be 75-25 rather than 50-50 are, in the main, two in number. First, I think that recognition should be given-and a 75-25 split would accord that recognition-to the fact that a great many people who might be

regarded as disabled persons are covered by provincial moneys of one kind or another; and if they are covered by grants in the form of mothers allowance, assistance from the province or from the municipality or are in various homes, they are excluded from receiving assistance under the legislation which is now before us. As I say, I think that recognition should be given to the fact that a great deal of provincial and municipal money is going to the assistance of persons who are disabled or incapacitated in one way or another. My other reason for urging a 75-25 split rather than 50-50 is, as I indicated at an earlier stage, that it would make it possible for the provinces with their more limited resources to pay their share of a higher allowance and their share of an allowance that might start at an earlier age.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the minister as to the age at which the allowance would start. Mr. Chairman, since the adjournment of the discussion of this clause yesterday, I, together with my parliamentary assistant, have had an opportunity to consider the suggestions which were made by the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The committee will remember that the clause is one having to do with the appointment of peace officers. The point raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert was that the national harbours board should not take unto itself greater powers than the Canadian National Railways have taken in the appointment of such peace officers, and that the appointment should be made by a judge of the superior court or the county court judge. Perhaps the point is well taken, and it will be possible to propose an amendment in the course of the next few minutes which I think will meet the difficulty.
However, after very careful consideration, it has not been possible to meet the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I refer to the mileage over which the peace officers would have jurisdiction, and the suggestion that it should be reduced from 25 miles to 5 miles or 1 mile. There is a serious difficulty in the city of Montreal which could well arise in other cities such as Vancouver. It has been brought to my attention that the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines gave careful consideration to this matter and saw fit to recommend the bill to the house with an amendment reducing the jurisdiction from 50 miles to 25 miles. That committee gave it careful consideration, and so did we, and we feel that there should not be a further reduction. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we now come to consideration of clause 3 as amended and the point which worries us is that the national harbours board under this clause will have the power to have constables appointed who will have jurisdiction 25 miles beyond the national harbours board property in any direction.
We believe that that is both unnecessary and unwise, and I propose to move an amendment cutting that distance down from 25 to 1 mile. It is significant, Mr. Chairman, that if we turn to the Railway Act, which the minister has followed in making the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Prince Albert, we find that a judge appointing a constable under the Railway Act for a railway company can appoint that constable only to act on and along such railway.
These qualifying words can be found in the last line of subsection 1 of section 456 of the Railway Act. In other words, the judge appoints a constable to act only on and along that particular railway.
Now, it is worth while to see just what powers the harbour commissioners and the national harbours board have had in the past in the appointment of constables. For example, I find this provision contained in the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners Act, chapter 54 of the 1913 statutes, under section 19, which gives the power to make bylaws, and we find that the corporation may make bylaws for the following purposes:
(b) To regulate and control navigation and all works or operations within the harbour and to appoint constables and other officers to enforce the same or to enforce the provisions of any statute or marine regulation.
Obviously the power there was merely to appoint constables to act on the property of the Vancouver harbour commissioners and to enforce any statutes or marine regulations which applied to the harbour commissioners' property.
I have not had an opportunity of looking up the acts setting up the other harbour commissions, but I presume that much the same powers were granted in each case. The intention obviously was that these harbour commissions could appoint someone to look after their own property and the goods passing over that property.
Then, when the national harbours board was set up in 1936 and given power to take
National Harbours Board Act over the control of the seven national harbours in Canada, we find that it was given power under section 4 as follows:
The board may employ such professional, technical and other officers, clerks and employees as it may deem necessary for the proper conduct of its business.
Under that authority the board, at least in Vancouver, and I presume the same is true of the other national ports, had the power to appoint a small local force to keep order on the national harbours board property, in much the same way as the C.P.R. and C.N.R. have railway constables to keep order on their property. But the force is not a trained one in any sense of the word. In effect, that police force is a sort of glorified watchman service, though, of course, it fulfils a very useful function.
But now the national harbours board is seeking greatly to extend various powers by the amendments in the bill, and is asking for power to set up a police force. I mentioned in the committee that their constables were not trained, and I think the parliamentary assistant, or one of the officials of the national harbours board, said, "Well, we are going to give them some training". That would mean that in Vancouver we will have another police force right in the business section of the city, despite the fact that we have an efficient city police force now. The R.C.M.P. are policing all of the province outside of the cities which have their own police force and they are doing an excellent job. Why on earth should a harbour police force be set up now?
There is no objection to their carrying on their duties within the national harbours board property or within a reasonable distance of that property, but this bill, if passed, will give them the power to appoint persons to act as police officers for a distance of 25 miles from the national harbours board property in every direction. That would mean that in Vancouver the harbour police could go into any part of the city and make arrests and, in effect, act as ordinary constables.
Surely there is no justification for setting up a duplicate police force of this kind. We do not want the harbour police running around our city making arrests. If arrests have to be made in the city, let them be made by the city police, and let the harbour police co-operate with the city police and have the arrests made through them.
There is no reason at all why the citizens of Vancouver should be subjected to a harbour police force coming into their homes or acting in the same way as the regular city police force.

National Harbours Board Act

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: This bill does no such thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
But this bill does do such a thing. If something is stolen from the harbours board property then the harbour police would have the same right as the city police to come into the city and arrest the person who is alleged to have stolen the goods. Not only that, the distance is so great that they can arrest people in the New Westminster area. New Westminster is about 12 miles from Vancouver. By giving Vancouver harbour police jurisdiction over 25 miles, you bring about the result that these Vancouver harbour police can walk over on to another harbour commission's property and make arrests. Fortunately the New Westminster harbour commission does not come under the National Harbours Board Act. They do not have to carry that load. But here they are going to be in a position where the Vancouver harbour police can make arrests on the New Westminster harbour commission's property.
I submit that there is absolutely no reason for establishing a police force with that jurisdiction. We need only go back to the Railway Act, and there we find just what sort of power should be given to a police force of this kind. Section 457 of the Railway Act, under the heading of "Territorial limits and powers," contains these provisions:
(1) Every constable so appointed, who has taken such oath or made such declaration, may act as a constable for the preservation of the peace, and for the security of persons and property against unlawful acts
(a)	on such railway, and on any of the works belonging thereto:-
We have no objection to these harbour police having jurisdiction over harbours board property. No one is questioning the wisdom of going that far. The section continues:
(b)	on and about any trains, roads, wharfs, quays, landing places, warehouses, lands and premises belonging to such company, whether the same are in the county, city, town, parish, district or other local jurisdiction within which he was appointed or in any other place through which such railway passes, or in which the same terminates, or through or to which any railway passes which is worked or leased by such company: and-
The minister will notice that again the power is confined to the railway.
-(c) in all places not more than a quarter of a mile distant from such railway.
If the railway police who are a proper police force-and who are a great deal better trained and much better qualified than this other police force is going to be

are to be restricted to one-quarter of a mile from railway property, why should the harbour police be given jurisdiction over 25 miles? That is a move the justification for which I cannot see.


The minister today mentioned that he needs this power in Montreal. It may be that in Montreal the harbours board cannot get co-operation from the city police or from the provincial police. I would not be surprised to learn that that is the case, that the harbours board police do not get on with the other police, and hence want the power to run out into Montreal, 25 miles from harbours board territory, and to make arrests. But that condition does not exist in Vancouver and I do not believe it exists in any of the other national ports of Canada.
If there is a situation to be met in Montreal, and the Montreal members in this chamber are willing to have the harbours police making arrests in the city of Montreal outside of harbours board property, then let us restrict this 25-mile provision to the port of Montreal. There is no reason why the six other ports should be penalized in order to meet a situation which may or may not exist in the port of Montreal. This is one country, but there is no reason why one port should force a thing like this on six other ports. If there is such a thing as majority rule, surely it should apply in this case. The national harbours board is taking this drastic power in violation of a principle governing the enforcement of our Canadian laws. I suggest that no governmental body should be given police jurisdiction over other territory for a distance of 25 miles.
I therefore move:
That clause 3 of BUI No. 421 be amended by deleting the word "twenty-five" where it appears in the thirteenth line of the proposed section 4A. (1) and the word "one" be substituted therefor.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise in support of the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I listened carefully to all the arguments that were presented in the committee of the House of Commons that studied the bill. I have also listened carefully to both the minister and the parliamentary assistant. Neither of them has yet, to my satisfaction, brought forward any argument in support of the reason why the harbour police should have all the authority of a police officer under the Criminal Code to a distance of 25 miles beyond the property which is owned by the harbours board or is administered by it.
I completely fail to understand how the minister can differentiate between the rights, the responsibilities or the jurisdiction of the special constables of the harbours board and those of the constables on the railways of this dominion. We have in the city of Vancouver the termini of the Canadian Pacific

Railway, the Canadian National Railways and the Great Northern Railway. They all have their own constables under the terms of the Railway Act. What are the duties of those special constables? Their duties are responsibility for the protection of the property of those three railways and the protection of goods in transit over those railways so long as they are on the properties of those railways. I have yet to hear of any request being made by the railways or any suggestion being made by the government that the authority which has been there for years should be changed and that those special constables who are guarding the property of the railways and the goods in transit over them should have their jurisdiction extended beyond a quarter of a mile, as it now exists under the present act.
That being the case, and no suggestion of altering that situation having been made, whence comes the differentiation as far as the harbours board property is concerned? Harbours board property is at a port and the duty of any constable is the protection of the property owned or administered by the harbours board and the protection of the goods in transit at that time in the possession of the harbours board. With regard to their complete responsibilities, the harbours board police are absolutely no different from the special constables of the railway systems of Canada. Then on what basis, on what line of logic and reasoning-when their duties and responsibilities are absolutely identical -should harbours board policemen have authority under the Criminal Code as peace officers for a distance of 25 miles outside harbours board property while the railway constables have jurisdiction only up to one-quarter of a mile from a railway. It does not make sense in any way, shape or form. I am therefore heartily in accord- and if I had my way it would be done-with bringing the jurisdiction of constables of the harbours board in line with the provisions of the Railway Act. However, I think my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is trying to do as was suggested by the minister yesterday. He is trying to be reasonable. He has come up with a compromise. His amendment will mean that harbours board policemen will have jurisdiction extending three-quarters of a mile farther than the jurisdiction of the railway police.
There is another phase which I think should be mentioned, the possibility of a clash of jurisdictions. When the police authorities are doing a good job and carrying out their responsibilities in a city such as Vancouver,
National Harbours Board Act I think such duties should be left to them. If my experience counts for anything, when any breach of the Criminal Code takes place on railway or harbours board property it is the local police force that does the investigating and lays the charge. I can remember when two policemen were shot on railway property in the city of Vancouver a few years ago. It was not the railway police who undertook the investigation. It was the local Vancouver police force. When it comes to areas outside harbours board or railway property, I think it is a matter for the local police force. If it should happen that an instance occurs, such as we were told about both here and in the committee, where one city police force does not co-operate, that is really no reason for causing a disturbance in the other harbour cities of the dominion.
I have only heard one reason given why the harbours board wants authority over such a large area beyond the property of the board. That was the reason that the harbours board either owns or operates a bridge in Montreal and that unless they have this jurisdiction they cannot catch a speeding car or motorcycle if it happens to get away from the end of the bridge. To me that is a pretty poor reason to ask for a change of the type being sought in section 3. Moreover, there is also this point. Even if an infraction of the law involving stolen goods does take place on property owned or administered by the harbours board, the policeman cannot conduct a search without obtaining a search warrant. Therefore he has to go before a justice of the peace or magistrate of the county or town before he can search.
Having to do that, surely right then and there is the time to place the actual responsibility in the hands of the local police force, whether city or provincial, which enforces justice in the harbour city. For all these reasons, having listened very carefully to the minister and the parliamentary assistant, I say that the provision in section 3 for the extension of power to a point 25 miles distant from harbours board property is unnecessary and unjust. The case in support of the amendment rests on the fact that the responsibility of the harbour police is the same as that of the railway police in whose case it has been found satisfactory to limit their jurisdiction to a quarter of a mile. I support the amendment.

So far as the jurisdiction of a police officer of a railway where the line runs from one end of Canada to the other is concerned, probably it is consistent that it should not extend beyond the quarter of a mile limit, but here the position is not at all the same. Men have taken property from the national

harbours board, have been sought beyond the limits of the property and because the warrants were not backed in the proper jurisdiction it was necessary in more than one case to lose the benefit of the law in respect of the person who was being chased.

I accept my hon. friend's
correction. I was under the impression he had a different idea of the application. But what is so abnormal about the fact that a peace officer should be able to seek within the required jurisdiction, particularly if an offence has to do with the administration of board property or of persons subject to the jurisdiction of the national harbours board? It seems to me it is not beyond reason, when there are millions of dollars spent, voted by this house, to see that that money is protected.
These officers are not going to clash with the other officers of the city of Montreal or the city of Vancouver. How can they, unless warrants are made out at the instance of the national harbours board officers, and at the instance of the local police for the same offence? That I am sure will not be done. The national harbours board has been in existence since 1935, and the administration of the act by the officers has been fair, just and reasonable. I feel that we can count on the officers of the board to use their common sense, to use their judgment, not only in the city of Montreal but in the city of Vancouver as well. If this section is given a fair trial, I believe it will be workable and that hon. members will not have any reason to complain about any extraordinary power. I want to reassure the house that it is not the intention to take extraordinary powers, that extraordinary powers are not being taken under this section, but that powers are being taken for the protection of the property of the board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF PROVISION RESPECTING DISTRIBUTION OF NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall make a brief explanation. This bill is being introduced as a result of representations received by the government from the Periodical Press Association on behalf of Canadian publishers, to the effect that the proposed amendment will be of benefit to them.
At the present time, Canadian publishers, in order to enjoy the reduced statutory rates on copies of their publications going to subscribers, must post such copies at the post office in the place in which the office of publication is situated.
The publishers' representations are to the effect that if more than one point of mailing was permitted they could forward their publications in certain instances by bus, by truck or by air cargo to other centres for local mailing and thus afford a faster delivery to their subscribers in different parts of the country. This would be an advantage to them in their competition with United States publications.
Apart from being an advantage to publishers, the proposed amendment could conceivably result in some saving to the Post Office Department, as we would not have to pay certain transportation charges in any instance where a publisher took advantage of this suggested procedure. In so far as the Post Office Department is concerned, we recommend the adoption of the legislation.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF PROVISION RESPECTING DISTRIBUTION OF NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as there are questions we will wish to ask at the committee stage, I do not propose at this time to discuss the matter at length. However, there are certain questions which, because of the nature of the bill, particularly its brevity and its apparent innocence-a feature which, may I say, we always suspect-we will want to ask. We will want to know precisely what the effect of the bill will be.
First of all, we will want to know just how many centres the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) might designate as areas to which bulk shipments might be made, in respect of any one national publication. Is this going to be a matter of several centres within a province, or the main terminal points in the
Post Office Act
provinces across Canada? We would also like to know whether or not this change in the regulation will have any effect on the content of any periodical. Will it alter in any way the rules which now exist with regard to the advertising these publications are permitted to accept?
When I ask this, I have in mind the fact of course that certain publications will be in a preferred position, by reason of their being able to get their publications into the field at distant points days quicker than otherwise they would be able to do. That is an advantage in competing for advertising in the general advertising field as against the United States publications which now enjoy that privilege.
There is also the general question of revenue. In what way will the revenue of the Post Office Department be affected by this change? Another general point into which we shall want to inquire rather closely is just what is the difference in this matter of the shipment of publications between daily newspapers and periodicals. The minister will recall that when we were speaking on the first item of his estimates I addressed a question to him with regard to the shipment of newspapers to distant points by T.C.A. in passenger seats. If I remember correctly the minister at that time told me that that was a matter strictly between the newspaper itself and T.C.A. I notice that this bill does say both newspapers and periodicals. If regulations exist which prohibit the bulk shipment of newspapers and periodicals to distant points, there to be broken down and mailed, then I should like to know under what regulation the newspapers are permitted to bulk ship, and if that permission is granted to them-possibly this is a question which would more properly be directed to the department which handles T.C.A., but nevertheless the minister, having some connection with it, must also know the answer- under what terms is T.C.A. permitted to occupy passenger seats with these newspapers, certainly to the inconvenience of the travelling public and possibly also to the detriment of their actual safety. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that in bringing up that point I am probably on the borderline. The Postmaster General has very definite responsibility in this regard because of the connection which his department has with the dissemination of this material from coast to coast. With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, we shall rest until the bill gets to the committee stage, when we shall press for answers to these and other questions.

The other purpose they achieve is that they get the cheap rate of postage provided for periodicals under section 11 of the Post Office Act because they are mailing their periodical at the point declared to be the point of publication.
Section 11 of the Post Office Act now requires that a periodical, in order to enjoy the cheap rate of postage, must be mailed in the postal area in which its office of publication is located.
Now, I agree with the Secretary of State that they are just gettting around the law technically but not in spirit, but in order to do this it is now costing Maclean's magazine a considerable sum of money-I understand it is of the order of $20,000 to $25,000 a year- to truck its periodicals from Toronto to Montreal.

At the present time all the issues of Maclean's magazine are being trucked to Montreal and mailed from there. If the bill passes they will be mailed from Toronto to western Canada. So far as the post office is concerned, there is practically no difference involved in that change. Issues for western Canada will be carried from Toronto to Sudbury or Capreol and then on west instead of being carried from Montreal to Sudbury or Capreol and then on west. Mr. Chairman, as hon. members know, this bill has been before the veterans affairs committee and there were quite a number of amendments proposed. I might say that amendments have been made which were more or less agreeable to the majority of the committee, with the exception of amendments relative to clause 2.
As hon. members will recall, when the resolution introducing this bill was before the house strenuous objection was taken to the principle as set out in clause 2 that the salaries of the commissioners be fixed by order in council. That is entirely contrary to the principle which has been followed since the inception of the act.
Certain groups of veterans organizations appeared before the committee and gave evidence, and the Canadian Legion, which as hon. members know speaks for the great majority of veterans across Canada, took 83276-358
Pension Act
very serious objection to clause 2. I might add that all the opposition members on the committee and one member of the government shared that serious objection to the principle as set out in clause 2. I do not feel I should review all the objections which were taken in committee at this time. They are already on record in this house and on the record of the veterans affairs committee. The chief objection taken was that it infringed the basic principle of the Canadian Pension Act in that it took away the independence of the commission as far as this matter was concerned.
I mentioned a moment ago that since the inception of this act the salaries of commissioners have been fixed by parliament. Under this new clause they would be fixed by order in council. The members of that commission sit and hear evidence which has to do almost entirely with the granting of pensions, and they hear that evidence for and against the granting of a pension before arriving at their decision, in the same fashion as a judge hears evidence and makes his decision. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 466, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (laying of information).
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when this bill was introduced and given first reading on May 28, its purpose is to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to make it clear that a trade union or an individual, on the one hand, or an employer or an employers' organization, on the other hand, has the right to lay an information or complaint under the act. Those who may have familiarized themselves with this

Industrial Relations
matter will probably realize that as section 45 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act now stands it is quite clear that a prosecution for an offence under the act may be brought against a trade union or against an employers' organization.
I think it is fair to say that most of us who are interested in this legislation have assumed that the opposite was also the case, namely, that it was possible for actions under the act to be brought by a trade union or by an employers' organization. I indicated on May 28 that a recent court decision has created some uncertainty and ambiguity with respect to whether an information or complaint can be laid by an aggrieved trade union against an employer. Accordingly, the purpose of the bill is to amend section 45 so as to clear up this uncertainty.
In view of the fact that in introducing this measure I made reference to a recent court decision I think it would be only fair that I indicate to the house the decision that I had in mind and its terms. It is not a very lengthy one so I think I had better read it to the house, although I should point out that there are sections of the decision that do not bear on the point that the bill seeks to correct. Nevertheless, since it is a legal point I think the decision should be on the record in full. It is a judgment given by Mr. Justice A. M. Campbell of the Court of Queen's Bench and was delivered at Winnipeg on April 6, 1954. I have a copy which has been furnished to me by the deputy prothon-otary of the Court of Queen's Bench, Winnipeg, so I have the correct terms of the judgment. It reads as follows:
This is an application in chambers for an order that Emil Walterson and Laundry and Dry Cleaning Workers' Union, 306 Donalda Building "be prohibited from taking any further proceedings" against the accused applicant in ten prosecutions (informations) laid under the Criminal Code for alleged violations of sections 4 (1), 4 (2) (a), 4 (2) (b) and 4 (3) of the Manitoba Labour Relations Act, S.M. 1948, chapter 27.
I am of the opinion that an application for an order of prohibition is the appropriate procedure in this case. It permits careful examination of the twenty-five exhibits filed, fifteen of which require study. This would not have been possible in a stated case.
This is a case where prohibition should lie. An application for prohibition based upon alleged defects on the face of the proceedings before a magistrate should not be affected by the prospect of an amendment being made to the information by which such proceedings were begun. There is no proper informant in any of the informations. The union was not the "aggrieved person", neither is Emil Walterson.
In any event, if the real prosecutor is Emil Walterson there is no consent to "institute" these proceedings. On the other hand, if the real prosecutor is the union, then it cannot be an informant, even acting through its president. Section 46(1) of the statute provides for a trade union or an

employers' organization being informed "against" i.e., of being an "accused". I am unable to find any section of the statute allowing either of them to be an informant.
Furthermore, in the proceedings before the magistrate, the so-called permission (consent) must stand alone. I am of the opinion that the so-called permission (consent) cannot serve the purpose intended in these proceedings. I do not think it is necessary to deal with the other arguments advanced by counsel.
An order of prohibition will go. Costs to the applicant.
As I have already indicated, that is the judgment given by Mr. Justice A. M. Campbell on April 6, 1954. May I make it clear that this judgment related to a matter that arose under the Manitoba labour relations act. Some hon. members may ask what that has got to do with our Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. The point is that the issues which arose in this case related to section 46, subsection 1, of the Manitoba labour relations act, which is identical word for word, jot for jot and tittle for tittle, with section 45, subsection 1 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
In other words if a court decision is made, and if such a decision stands, which places a certain interpretation on the words of section 46, subsection 1, of the Manitoba labour relations act, I think it follows that the same interpretation would be held to apply to the section in the federal act which is spelled out in exactly the same words. It is because of the fear that the judgment rendered by Mr. Justice Campbell might have an effect on labour relations generally, including the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, that those interested in these matters feel that what appears to be a defect or weakness in our labour law should be corrected.
May I also point out that much of what I read in quoting Mr. Justice Campbell's judgment in full does not have an immediate bearing on the issue which is presented in my bill. I merely read the whole judgment so that it might be a matter of record. What is significant in Mr. Justice Campbell's judgment is something that some lawyers might refer to as in the nature of an obiter dictum. It is this portion:
Section 46(1) of the statute provides for a trade union or an employers' organization being informed "against" i.e., of being an "accused". I am unable to find any section of the statute allowing either of them to be an informant.
That is the crux of the judgment, namely, that the wording of the Manitoba labour relations act, with the identical language in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, makes it possible for a trade union or an employers' organization to be informed against, but according to the learned judge it

does not make it possible for a trade union or an employers' organization to initiate an action under that statute even though it may regard itself as aggrieved under the terms of this legislation.

speechtext: If that was the crux of the judgment, it was not an obiter dictum.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

My hon. friend, I would say, has made a point. Perhaps I could straighten it out this way. Maybe it was not the crux of the argument, so far as this application was concerned. It may have been that the learned judge allowed an order of prohibition on the basis of other defects which were spelled out in the judgment, but so far as labour generally is concerned, in relation to matters that may arise in the future under our labour laws, the crux of this judgment is in the sentence I have just quoted. The smile on the minister's face seems to suggest that I have straightened that out, so perhaps I may read it again.
Section 46 (1) of the statute-
The reference is to the Manitoba statute, but the language is exactly the same as we find in section 45 (1) of the federal statute.
-provides for a trade union or an employers' organization being informed "against" i.e., of being an "accused". I am unable to find any section of the statute allowing either of them to be an informant.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those who are interested in this case, both because of their interest in this particular case and because of their interest in the labour laws of this country, felt at first that the judge had made an error, and that his decision should be appealed. The latest word I have is that that decision on the part of those interested has been altered although it may be they are still planning to appeal to a higher court. Certainly labour lawyers and counsel who advised the trade union bodies, both locally at Winnipeg and nationally here at Ottawa, are of the opinion that the learned judge may have something in so far as the interpretation of the wording of the law is concerned. None of us thought that the law was meant to have that interpretation, that trade unions or employers' organizations could be informed against but could not lay an information. It is because it appears to be. a defect that we felt consideration should be given to making the necessary amendment to section 45, subsection 1, of the labour code. Perhaps so that this record might be complete and clear to those who are interested,
Industrial Relations
I should put on the record section 45, subsection 1, of the labour code as it now stands. It reads as follows:
A prosecution for an offence under this act may be brought against an employers' organization or a trade union and in the name of the organization or union and for the purpose of such a prosecution a trade union or an employers' organization shall be deemed to be a person, and any act or thing done or omitted by an officer or an agent of an employers' organization or trade union within the scope of his authority to act on behalf of the organization or union shall be deemed to be an act or thing done or omitted by the employers' organization or trade union.
Bearing in mind the point I am trying to make, hon. members will see that if, as I contend, there is a weakness or defect in this subsection it is in the first line or two thereof. I refer to the portion of that subsection where it says:
A prosecution for an offence under this act may be brought against . . .
And so on. Our contention is that to cure the defect the wording should be that a prosecution for an offence under this act may be brought "by or against ..." All that is needed to ensure protection either way, if either party is aggrieved, is to insert the words "by or" in the appropriate place, just before the word "against". Those who have looked at this matter feel it would be well to make sure there are no loopholes, no point not covered, and just to do that section 45 should be further amended by adding a new subsection 3 which would read:
(3) Any information or complaint in respect of any prosecution under this act may be laid by an employer, an employers' organization, trade union or person claiming to be aggrieved under this act.
In presenting this bill, Mr. Speaker, it is my belief we are not asking for anything new. We are not asking for anything we have not assumed to be part of the labour law, but rather we are asking that the necessary step be taken to correct what appears to be a defect, in view of the decision rendered by Mr. Justice Campbell at Winnipeg to which I have made reference. I present the matter to the house hoping that favourable consideration will be given to this request of those who are interested in the correction of this defect, and that the legislation be made to read so that it will carry what we thought was the intent, namely that the aggrieved person or aggrieved body, be it a trade union or an employers' organization, should be able to lay an information under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.

The Leader of the Opposition referred to a member of his family who is 14, and I could refer to some members of mine, all of whom are younger than that and who sometimes display more wisdom than, in my very prejudiced view, is sometimes displayed by some legislators in this chamber- if I may be permitted to say that.

But the reason I was impressed by the argument of the Leader of the Opposition-indeed, I had intended to make it myself, had he not got there first- was that it does seem to me that before we change the voting age we should change the age at which people who would vote would have full legal capacity. The age of 21 years is that at which one can sue and be sued on one's own account, and the age at which one assumes full legal obligations. As I conceive it, voting is one of the most important of the obligations of a full citizen. If there is to be a change in the voting age, as to the wisdom of which I think there can be two opinions, and about which up to now I must confess I have not formed any very strong views, it seems to me the other step ought to be taken first.
There is another danger in this kind of proposal. It seems to me it is the kind to which the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), and perhaps to an even greater extent the hon. member who represents Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), are prone, and that is

what I might call the auction type of legislation. That is to say, someone in the house makes an offer and, with no early hope of having to accept any responsibility, the hon. gentlemen can always outbid.

In fact, most of the argument advanced in support of this measure by most of those who supported it was, if my memory serves me correctly, that we ask people to fight at the age of 18, when there is fighting to be done, and that therefore if they are old enough to fight they should be old enough to vote.
One hon. member-and I think it was my fellow Manitoban, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras)-pointed out that enlistments are permitted into the army, not at the age of 18 but at 17J. So that probably there should be an amendment, if that is to be the main argument. I do not think the fact that 18 years is already the law in Saskatchewan is any very compelling reason for most of us in the house to adopt this as a national measure.

a quarter million to half a million extra electors, on to the rolls it would mean that the cost of holding elections would be considerably increased. I doubt very much whether the results of elections would be changed to any material degree. They might be occasionally; it is a little hard to say. But it seems to me that if we have-as we have in this country-universal suffrage for persons 21 years of age and over, we do in fact in a general election get an adequate and a fair cross-section of the whole population, and that after all is what the purpose of elections is.
I do think also it is undesirable to tamper with these conventional ways of doing things unless-and this is a very important qualification-one is really convinced that by changing them definite improvement will be made.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Assiniboia felt that if this change were made it would be of benefit to one particular party rather than another. I do not think he did. Personally, I do not think it would. On balance I do not think it will have very much effect of any kind, except to increase the number of votes cast, increase the number of voters, increase the cost of elections and possibly, too, impose on a lot of Canadians the duty of making up their minds about questions on which two or three years more reflection would probably enable them to reach conclusions which would be more valid.
I go back again to my own personal experience. I think I was just as intelligent at the age of 18 as I was at the age of 21, but in the interval I had had a certain amount of experience, or a certain number of experiences, sir, and for some of us experience does alter our outlook, and in some cases it does widen our horizons; it does in some cases add to our knowledge. All these things, it seems to me, are desirable.
I would not like to be misunderstood. I am not one of those neo-fascists who believe that only the good or the virtuous or the wise should be allowed to vote. I think it is just as important for those who are not quite so good and those who are not quite so wise to be allowed to vote, too.

I do not
intend to discuss this measure at any great length. I agree with the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) that if the change in voting age which is proposed by this measure does come into effect I would not consider it to be a matter of world-shattering importance. But it is a question, as he has suggested, of judgment on which members from various parts of the house might feel they can express their honest views.
I have listened with a good deal of interest to some of the arguments that he has advanced, and they have included some relation to his own experience as a young voter. I would feel that if we had an election in this country every year there would be a good deal more validity to his argument than appears to me to be at the present time. I might, for example, interject my own particular experience on the first occasion on which I had a chance to cast a ballot. It so happened that the federal election was held when I had reached or just passed the age of 20, which meant, as you can readily see, that before I cast my first vote in an election I had reached the very mature age of 24 or 25. This question should be considered in part at least from that point of view. I have long felt that one of the most disconcerting aspects of our society is the lack of interest which a large percentage of citizens take in the public affairs of the country.
Frankly, my principal reason for rising to support this measure is that I believe it would serve to stimulate in the young people in the country reaching manhood and womanhood a greater interest in the public affairs of our country. I base my reason for that in part at least upon the fact that a great many of our young people in the country are finishing their schooling at approximately the age of 18, and that in most of our modern schools today a certain amount of time is spent in arousing in the students an interest in the institution of government and in various other aspects of public affairs. If it were possible, assuming that an election followed shortly after the graduation of students from high school, to have them participate in an election to the extent of at least casting a vote, then I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, there

is a likelihood that their interest would be stimulated and would continue. At least there is a greater likelihood than if they were faced with a period of years during which they would have to wait until they reached the age of 25 without having the stimulus of an election to interest them in a decision that is important so far as our national policies are concerned.
With regard to the argument advanced by the Secretary of State to the effect that along with this provision should go the right to assume full legal responsibility in every other aspect of life, I think I would agree with his point if he were to limit that to the right, for example, to stand for election and be elected as a member of parliament. But it seems to me on the basis of his own argument that the net result of allowing people of this age to vote would not be to cause any great change in the political spectrum of this country. His argument allows a good deal of ground for the discredited point that that right should not be given unless full legal responsibility in every other sense was allowed. I commend the points I have raised to the attention of the house before we are called upon to make a decision on this measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE VOTING AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) speaks again there are just one or two remarks I would like to make on the general principle involved in this very interesting discussion which has arisen regarding the voting age. I am sure none of us here would wish to belittle or criticize or in any way discuss the lack of ability of our 18-year-olds, nor in any way mention their lack of wisdom or maturity. We all know that the young people in Canada probably have a broader outlook, certainly a greater opportunity for education, and probably a wider experience in the light of present-day living than they had a decade or two ago.
The argument has been raised that, having reached the age of 18, they have enough experience, wisdom and maturity to make
Canada Elections Act
it possible for them to vote intelligently, and hence this bill has been introduced. I assume that that is the only basis on which this bill can be justified. Well, the age-old view has been, of course, that 21 is the age of, I think it is called, discretion. That view has a long history and has existed, I suppose, ever since we have had the system of common law introduced in England. Ever since that system was set up 21 has been considered the age when one becomes legally responsible for one's actions. It is the only age at which a person can enter into a binding contract, and that is a basic premise that has been in effect for, I suppose, well nigh on 1,000 years up to this time.
Presumably there is a very sound basis for that legal belief, and it is not something that you can discard lightly. That is not to say that making the voting age 18 is directly related to that legal right, duty or responsibility, but it certainly is an encroachment on that principle.
As I have already said, it would take a very careful estimate of the situation before one could bring oneself to vote for this particular measure. If my memory serves me right, when the hon. member for Assiniboia was introducing this bill he said he felt- and he can correct me if I am wrong-that our 18-year-olds are better educated today than they were at one time and they were now in a position to vote intelligently at that age. Apropos of that there is a great deal of confusion existing in educational circles regarding the education our youth are now receiving. In Ontario last year the Ontario Educational Association conducted a survey of the province of Ontario to determine just what happened to school children after they started school, what qualifications they received, from which courses they finally graduated, and what happened to them up to the time of leaving university.
They found out that out of every 100 children who commenced elementary school, only 13 ended up with any sort of graduation certificate from high school. In other words, in Ontario only 13 out of 100 graduated with a senior matriculation in high school, and since it is a very progressive and rich province I presume that figure might well be applicable to the other nine provinces. I have no way of knowing, of course, whether that is true, but you cannot merely assume because the opportunity for education is there that that opportunity is always taken. Certainly if you are using that as a criterion I would submit that that criterion is not a valid one because 13 is certainly nowhere near a majority of the youth who

Canada Elections Act
should graduate. The others leave school, I presume, at the average school leaving age of 16J or 17.
Is it too much to say that they need the four years between 17 and 21, or the five years between 16 and 21, to feel their way, get their feet on the ground, and gain that experience which comes only with being in business and through the effort they must put forth to make a living? Is it too much to say that they need that four or five years to prepare their minds and to gain the necessary experience and information to vote intelligently?
It seems to me that is the only way in which we can tackle this problem. As I said, there has been a great deal of confusion in educational circles in Ontario regarding this particular problem and the plight of the student who is in high school, who leaves high school and goes on to university.
I know that of the 13 who graduate with a senior matriculation there are only three in Ontario who go on to university. Of that three, one quits, one fails and the other graduates, so we have an average now of one out of 100 children who go to elementary school in Ontario, graduate from there, and then finally graduate from university, according to the figures of the Ontario Educational Association in a survey they conducted in November, 1953.
With this in mind, and bearing in mind the views of other qualified people such as Dr. Hilda Neatby who, in her book, "Too Little for the Mind" created quite a furore, I think the situation certainly requires a great deal more study than we are able to give it, or can give it in this debate in the house at the present time. I would submit that the time is not ripe, the matter has not been sufficiently adjudicated upon, or the criterion on which we are going to change the voting age has not been sufficiently established for us to vote intelligently to change the voting age from 21 to 18 at this particular time.

I do not know, but probably my hon. friend still holds those ideas. However, he certainly would not advocate them now that women are important and have influence because they have the vote. To advocate anything of that kind would mean the disappearance of the advocate from any political scene.
From reading English history I remember the opposition to the universal franchise for persons 21 years of age and over when it was advocated in that country. I recall reading Lord Macaulay's speech in the House of Commons in opposition to the measure, wherein he told of the dreadful things that would happen to the British people if these uneducated workers were given the right to vote. However, they were given the right to vote and those dreadful things have not happened to the people of the United Kingdom. When women were given the right to vote in that country, they were not given the vote at the age of 21; they were given it at the age of 26. Although women are supposed to mature earlier than do men, they were not given the vote until they reached an age five years older than that at which men received the vote.
I think a good deal of nonsense is talked with regard to this matter of the age of discretion. In the Journal the other day, I saw a definition of "discretion". I am sorry that I forgot to bring it with me but I think it was to the effect that it is the age at which you find you cannot do the things you would like to do. It was something like that although it may not be just quite that. If it is not, it ought to be anyway.
I find that when a person becomes a member of the armed forces at the age of 18 or perhaps earlier, he is entitled to vote. If a person who becomes a member of the armed forces at the age of 18 is entitled to vote, what about the person who sets out to earn a livelihood for, say, his mother and the younger members of his family at the age of 18? I may say that there are many of them. Should not that boy or that girl be allowed to vote? Why all these fine distinctions? They have no validity at all. If the age of 21 has been set, as was said by the hon. member who preceded me, say for perhaps one thousand years, on what basis was it set? Who said that was the age where

men came to the point where they could choose right from wrong or when they should have the right to take part in government as mature human beings? It was something arbitrarily set by somebody. I do not know who the nincompoop was but I have no doubt that he was just as ill-advised as I would be if I said the age should be 17.
The hon. member who preceded me referred to Dr. Neatby's book. He is right. It caused a furore but I think that is all you can say for it. Whether there is any basis of knowledge or understanding underlying what she says is a question that is much debated.
I would suggest that we get down to earth and realize that our objection to this step is the old reluctance that has come down through the ages, the old habit of wishing to limit the franchise or participation in government to as few people as possible. The young people today at the age of 18- particularly those who have not had the opportunity to go to university but who have had to take up the responsibilities of citizens before they were 21-are entitled to the vote, and we should not refuse it to them.
